article.title: pnpm 12 Rewrites the Package Manager in Rust, Cutting Vercel's Turborepo Install Times by Up to 90.5%
article.summary: pnpm 12 replaces its Node.js and TypeScript core with a Rust rewrite while keeping pnpm 11's commands and lockfile format, and an independent Vercel benchmark found install times fell as much as 90.5%.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

pnpm has shipped pnpm 12, a rewrite of the JavaScript package manager's Node.js and TypeScript foundation into native Rust, according to [pnpm's official release announcement](https://pnpm.io/blog/releases/12.0) from lead maintainer Zoltan Kochan. "pnpm 12 is stable. It is a rewrite of pnpm in Rust. Upgrading should not feel like a migration," the announcement states, and pnpm says the commands, flags, settings, and lockfile format from pnpm 11 all carry over, with documentation covering both versions.

An independent benchmark cited by [Socket](https://socket.dev/blog/pnpm-12) found the change delivers substantial real-world gains: when Vercel upgraded its 21-project Turborepo workspace, which installs 1,670 packages, pnpm 12 cut median install times by 64.4% to 90.5% compared with pnpm 10.28 across six combinations of warm and cold stores, present and absent `node_modules`, and enabled or disabled lifecycle scripts.

## What We Know

- pnpm 12 is available now, released August 26, according to [Socket](https://socket.dev/blog/pnpm-12). Because npm's `latest` tag still points to the pnpm 11 line, users must opt in explicitly, as [pnpm's release notes](https://pnpm.io/blog/releases/12.0) instruct: "`latest` on npm still points at the pnpm 11 line, so install pnpm 12 from the `next-12` tag: `pnpm self-update next-12`." Homebrew, winget, Scoop, and Chocolatey do not yet offer the new version, per the same announcement.
- On pnpm's own benchmark fixture, a clean install fell from 8.2 seconds under the previous implementation to 5 seconds with Rust, and a repeated install with a warm cache, lockfile, and `node_modules` dropped from 472 milliseconds to 15 milliseconds, according to [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/pnpm-12-rust/).
- In Socket's report on the Vercel benchmark, the largest reduction came when `node_modules` was already present: install time fell from 1.476 seconds to 142 milliseconds with a warm store, and from 1.385 seconds to 141 milliseconds with a cold one. With both the store and `node_modules` absent and lifecycle scripts enabled, the median install time dropped from 9.850 seconds to 3.472 seconds. Those results came from 20 measured runs per version on the same Linux system, [Socket reported](https://socket.dev/blog/pnpm-12).
- The speed gains carry a tradeoff at startup. pnpm 12's native Corepack artifact is 47.3 MB, compared with 17.5 MB for pnpm 10.28, which [Socket found](https://socket.dev/blog/pnpm-12) makes an uncached Corepack startup 11.1% slower — though once cached, startup is 74.7% faster, a figure [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/pnpm-12-rust/) also confirmed independently. The combined pnpm store and `node_modules` footprint on [Socket's test system](https://socket.dev/blog/pnpm-12) fell 52.5%, from 3.891 GB to 1.850 GB.
- pnpm 12 changes how it resolves Git dependencies. For repositories hosted on GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket, a dependency specifier "now only says which repository you want," and resolution always goes through the host's canonical HTTPS URL rather than recording a machine-specific SSH transport in the lockfile, [pnpm's announcement explains](https://pnpm.io/blog/releases/12.0). Developers who need SSH for private repositories must configure a Git URL rewrite on their own machine.
- The release also drops the `pnpm install --resolution-only` flag, which [Socket](https://socket.dev/blog/pnpm-12) and [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/pnpm-12-rust/) both identify as the change most likely to break an existing CI pipeline; its former peer-dependency reporting role now belongs to the new `pnpm peers check` command.
- On cycle-heavy dependency graphs, pnpm 12 breaks cycles at a fixed point in the graph, producing byte-identical lockfiles regardless of install order, and [pnpm reports](https://pnpm.io/blog/releases/12.0) peer resolution runs two to three times faster while using about 25% less memory in those workspaces.
- New features include project-aware global bins — a globally installed `node`, `deno`, or `bun` now automatically runs the version pinned by the current project — and the ability for pnpm itself to install other package managers, including npm, Yarn, and Bun, each drawn from its own trusted source, with npm-published tools checked against npm's own signature before they run, [per pnpm's release notes](https://pnpm.io/blog/releases/12.0).
- pnpm also introduced an opt-in, proof-of-concept remote side-effects cache that can restore signed, organization-scoped build outputs instead of rerunning a dependency's lifecycle scripts on every machine; support is currently limited to Linux with glibc on x64 and Arm64, [pnpm says](https://pnpm.io/blog/releases/12.0).
- Kochan offered a blunt explanation for the timing of the rewrite: "It was faster to rewrite pnpm in Rust than to migrate to ESM," he said, according to [Socket](https://socket.dev/blog/pnpm-12), which also reported that he added he regretted moving pnpm 11 to ESM.

## What We Don't Know

- pnpm's own benchmark page previously compared pnpm 12 against Bun and Yarn using results from August 14 that predated several fixes to pnpm's benchmark harness, including a bug that let pnpm 12 reuse package metadata during supposedly clean installs and a separate error that gave Bun a warm cache while testing pnpm with a cold one, [Socket reported](https://socket.dev/blog/pnpm-12). pnpm has since removed Bun and Yarn from the public comparison on its site, and Kochan said he could not currently claim pnpm was the fastest package manager and would no longer publish comparisons with rivals other than npm — so how pnpm 12 stacks up against Bun and Yarn under corrected conditions remains unresolved.
- Frontend engineer Dennis Morello described the release as "a performance release wearing a major version number," according to [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/pnpm-12-rust/), but broader developer reaction to the migration effort — outside the specific commentary captured by InfoQ and Socket — has not yet been independently surveyed.

## Context

pnpm's move follows a broader pattern of JavaScript tooling shifting performance-critical code into Rust, a trend [Socket notes](https://socket.dev/blog/pnpm-12) already includes SWC, Biome, Oxc, Rolldown, and parts of Turbopack. Bun took a similar path in August, when it [shipped Bun 1.4 as its first stable release built on a Rust rewrite](/article/2026-08/20-bun-14-ships-as-first-stable-release-built-on-its-rust-rewrite-cutting-package-installs-30x-and-idle-cpu-5x), also emphasizing faster package installs. pnpm's own prior major update, pnpm 11, focused on a different problem entirely — a [24-hour default delay on newly published package releases](/article/2026-04/22-pnpm-11-rc-makes-a-24-hour-release-delay-the-default-turning-a-supply-chain-workaround-into-a-baseline) aimed at supply-chain security rather than install performance.
